subject: Cognitive Science
title: Theory of Mind
description: A short lesson to help you apply Theory of Mind.

hook.text: Sally hides a marble in a basket and leaves. Anne moves it. Where will Sally look? Kids under four fail.

buildup.text: Theory of mind is knowing that other people can hold beliefs different from your own.

discovery.text: The false belief test checks this: can a child understand someone else believes something wrong?

twist.text: Around age four, children pass. They realize Sally will look in the basket—where she left it.

climax.text: Without theory of mind, deception, empathy, and storytelling would be impossible.

punchline.text: Understanding others starts with knowing minds differ.

quiz.question: At what age do most children pass the false belief test?

details.summary: Theory of mind is the ability to attribute mental states like beliefs, desires, and intentions to others and understand that these may differ from your own. Most children develop this between ages three and five, as shown by the classic false-belief task.
details.whyItMatters: Theory of mind is essential for social life. It enables empathy, deception, persuasion, and cooperation. Its absence or delay is a key feature of autism spectrum conditions.
takeaways: Develops between ages three and five in most children
The false-belief task is the classic test of theory of mind
Essential for empathy, social interaction, and communication

faq.question: What is the false-belief task?
faq.answer: A child watches a puppet put a toy in box A, then leave. Another puppet moves the toy to box B. The child is asked where the first puppet will look. Children under four typically say box B, where the toy actually is, failing to represent the puppet's false belief.

faq.question: Is theory of mind absent in autism?
faq.answer: Not absent but often delayed or expressed differently. Many autistic individuals develop theory of mind but may do so later and rely more on explicit reasoning than intuitive understanding. The relationship between autism and theory of mind is more nuanced than once thought.
